segments.text: Welcome to your daily Robotics News Digest for October 16, 2026.
Today we cover breakthroughs in soft robotics, advanced manipulation, and the expansion of mobile systems.
Tune in for the latest developments.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Tesla patent reveals touch-sensitive skin for robot hands".
This report details a recent United States patent filed by Tesla concerning a method for creating touch-sensitive material for robotic hands that can detect contact, force, and pressure.
The patent describes a process involving printing tactile sensors onto flexible materials and then heat-forming these materials into three-dimensional shapes.

The proposed sensor employs overlapping conductive regions in two flexible layers to generate individual sensing points for pressure changes, utilizing capacitive and piezoresistive approaches with materials such as thermoplastic polyurethane.
This technology is suggested for application on robot fingertips, palms, and end-effectors to enhance dexterous manipulation capabilities.
The development suggests a pathway toward more sophisticated tactile feedback systems in advanced robotics.
From Robotics & Automation News, ETH Zurich scientists turn WUJI robotic hand into self-propelled mobile manipulator.
This report details a demonstration where a WUJI robotic hand achieved self-propelled locomotion by utilizing its fingers for crawling and recovering from falls.
The research involved training the hand to support its own weight and move independently without an external mobility system.
Reinforcement learning was employed for the training process, taking into account the unique characteristics of each finger to facilitate the learning.
This self-supported manipulator successfully executed manipulation tasks, including typing on a keyboard and pushing objects toward designated targets.
The work establishes the hand as a compact, mobile manipulator integrating both locomotion and manipulation functions.
This development indicates progress toward creating highly integrated, autonomous robotic systems capable of complex physical interaction.
From Robotics & Automation News, Pudu expands beyond service robots into semi-humanoids and quadrupeds.
This report details the company's recent development and exhibition of advanced robotic platforms.
At the IFA 2026 event, Pudu showcased the D7 semi-humanoid and the D5-W quadruped.
The D7 design prioritizes joint configuration for manipulation tasks instead of bipedal locomotion.
Furthermore, the D5-W demonstrated the capability to traverse complex terrain by dynamically switching between wheel and leg movement.
In addition to these new platforms, Pudu enhanced autonomy in existing commercial units, such as the CC1 Pro cleaning robot, enabling the system to assess and correct its cleaning procedures.
This diversification positions Pudu within emerging segments of industrial robotics development.
This expansion signals a growing trend toward more versatile and capable robotic forms across the technology sector.
From TheSequence, "The Sequence Robotics - Issue #952: One Brain, Many Bodies: Inside Skild AI's Robotics Bet"
reports on Skild AI's research into transferring robotic intelligence across different hardware.
The core finding is the exploration of separating intelligence from the physical body to enable more flexible robotic systems.
Skild AI's research focuses on motor adaptation, video-prompted task learning, and self-play to achieve this transferability.
The methodology involves training models to learn how to understand a body rather than relying on explicit engineering specifications.
The company is currently testing these capabilities against real-world constraints concerning speed, reliability, and safety in operational environments.
This approach aims to develop more adaptable robotic systems.
The ongoing testing indicates a path toward significantly more flexible and adaptable hardware solutions in the future.

From Robohub, Robot Talk Episode 166 – Evolving robot bodies and brains, with Rika Antonova reports on the integration of artificial intelligence to develop complementary robot hardware and algorithms.
This discussion explored the evolving nature of robot bodies and brains through AI integration.

The conversation featured Claire discussing work with Rika Antonova from the University of Cambridge, an Associate Professor specializing in co-design, automated algorithm discovery, and reinforcement learning in robotics.
Antonova possesses academic qualifications from Carnegie Mellon University and KTH Royal Institute of Technology, providing a strong foundation for the research presented.

The discussion detailed the process of utilizing artificial intelligence to create synergistic relationships between physical robot hardware and their computational brains, focusing on co-design methodologies and the discovery of automated algorithms within robotic systems.
This research emphasizes the ongoing evolution of how robot systems are conceived and programmed.
Future developments in this area will impact the trajectory of autonomous machine development.
From Humanoid.guide, PNDbotics Adam humanoid climbs 1 meter box, post claims.
This report details a demonstration where the Adam humanoid robot successfully climbed onto a one-meter high box.
The maneuver required the robot to analyze the obstacle, plan movements, and execute a sequence involving placing one foot on top before transferring its weight across its entire structure.
This ascent necessitated coordinated movement and precise weight transfer while maintaining overall balance.
This capability involved the robot supporting and raising its body during the climb.
The demonstration was shared in a post on LinkedIn by Space and Technology.
The successful demonstration indicates advancements in robotic locomotion and complex spatial reasoning.
Further research into these coordinated movements is anticipated within the artificial intelligence and robotics sector.
From Waymo Blog, "Hello Toronto! Waymo is En Route".
This report details the launch of Waymo's fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, targeting the first riders in 2028.
The rollout will proceed through a phased, safety-first methodology, beginning with the deployment of high-definition mapping and testing conducted with autonomous specialists.
Expansion plans involve a partnership with Element Fleet Management to generate employment opportunities within fleet management and operations.

Data indicates that the autonomous driver has been associated with significantly fewer serious crashes when compared to human drivers, based on analysis of over four hundred million autonomous kilometers traveled.
The service is designed to integrate with Toronto's current transportation infrastructure, emphasizing safety and accessibility.
This progression signals further integration of autonomous technology within established urban transit systems.
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: Logging and Observability Guide Review Part 4 | Cloud Robotics WG Meeting 2026-10-19"
reports on the ongoing review of the Logging and Observability guide by the Cloud Robotics Working Group.
The meeting, scheduled for Monday, October 19, 2026, aimed to finalize the first draft of the guide and prepare it for guest speaker review.
The session was structured into two time slots, 4:00 PM UTC and 5:00 PM UTC, to facilitate the necessary edits.
The objective of the meeting was to complete the editing process of the guide before distributing it to invited speakers for their feedback.
Information concerning access to the meeting and notifications is provided through designated channels.
This process ensures the refinement of standards within the robotics and software development community.
Future updates will reflect the guide's finalized status.
And that's all the circuits for today!
From tactile fingertips to future forms, keep those algorithms humming.
Thanks for tuning into the Robotics Digest.
See you tomorrow!
